section_1.title: The Combinatorial Bottleneck (Prerequisite Review)
section_1.content: Introduce the challenge of counting subsets with specific constraints (e.g., sum of elements divisible by k). Briefly refresh the concept of the formal power series: f(x) = ∑ a_n x^n, where a_n is the number of ways to form an object of size n.
section_1.example: A squirrel collecting acorns: How many ways can it collect an even number of acorns if it chooses from 3 types of piles?

section_2.title: The Roots of Unity Filter
section_2.content: Introduce the 'Filter Principle' using complex numbers. Show that for a generating function f(x), the sum of coefficients at indices divisible by k is given by (1/k) * Σ f(ω^j), where ω = e^(2πi/k). Visualize this as a 'Complex Phase Canceller' on a unit circle diagram.
section_2.example: Visualize the roots of unity ω as points rotating around a unit circle, showing how their sum cancels out terms that are not multiples of k.

section_3.title: Applying the Complex Tool
section_3.content: Demonstrate the integration of the Filter Principle. We substitute ω into the generating function f(x) = (1+x)^n to extract specific combinatorial sums.
section_3.example: Robot task distribution: A robot has n tasks; in how many ways can it select a number of tasks divisible by 3? We solve this by calculating (1/3) * [(1+1)^n + (1+ω)^n + (1+ω²)^n].

section_4.title: Synthesis and Geometric Intuition
section_4.content: Conclude by summarizing how complex numbers act as a sieve. Emphasize that rotating vectors in the complex plane effectively isolates valid combinatorial states.
section_4.example: The final animation shows the 'cancellation wave': multiple sine-like waves of different phases merging to leave only the desired counts behind.
